I notice that no specific symptom items were provided under the patient-reported symptoms section. However, I can work with the demographic and trauma information given, along with a PCL-5 score of 65, which indicates severe PTSD symptomatology. Let me construct a vignette that reflects a clinically coherent picture consistent with that severity level and the patient's background.

Rajinder came to the clinic on a Tuesday morning in late autumn, having been referred by his primary care physician after a routine appointment at which he had, for the first time in decades, said aloud that he was not sleeping and had not been for a very long time. He is seventy-nine years old, a lean man with careful posture and a habit of sitting with his hands folded on his knees, as though bracing for something. He worked for thirty-one years in a distribution warehouse on the outskirts of the city, pulling early morning shifts sorting freight, and he has not quite stopped thinking of himself as a warehouse worker even though his body forced him to reduce his hours three years ago. He was born in Punjab and came to the United States in his early thirties, after the war.

The war he refers to is the Indo-Pakistani conflict of 1971, in which Rajinder served as an infantry soldier on the western front. He was twenty-seven years old. Over the course of several weeks of active combat, he witnessed the deaths of men he had trained alongside, including a close friend who died beside him during a sustained artillery barrage on a position they had been ordered to hold. What Rajinder returns to, in memory and in sleep, is not the whole of that period but a specific sequence: the sound of incoming fire, the ground shaking, the moment he looked to his left and understood from what he saw that his friend was gone. He remembers the particular quality of the light that afternoon - flat, yellowish, the kind that precedes a dust storm - and the smell of smoke mixed with something metallic he has never been able to name precisely. He was not evacuated. He continued fighting. He has never spoken of this to his children, and his former wife, from whom he has been divorced for eighteen years, knew only that he had served and that he did not discuss it.

For most of the intervening decades, Rajinder managed. He worked. He was, by his own account, not a man given to complaint. But the warehouse, where he spent the bulk of his working life, presented him with a recurring difficulty he never named to anyone. The facility received large freight shipments by truck, and the hydraulic loading dock equipment produced, when engaged, a low concussive thud that reverberated through the concrete floor. On the days those deliveries arrived, Rajinder would find himself rigid at his station, his heart loud in his chest, scanning the middle distance for something he could not articulate. He developed the habit of volunteering for inventory tasks in the back of the building on delivery mornings, telling his supervisors he preferred the quieter work. No one questioned this. It became simply the way things were.

He had come to believe, in a formulation he could not quite put into words but felt with certainty, that what had happened to him in 1971 had left something permanently altered in him - not a wound exactly, but a change in the material of his character. He was certain that other men who had seen the same things had moved through their lives without this residue, and that his inability to do the same reflected something he preferred not to examine. He stopped attending the gurdwara regularly in his sixties, finding that the resonance of the ceremonial drums, which he had loved as a young man, now produced in him a discomfort he could not justify to himself or others. He told himself he was simply tired on Sunday mornings. Over time, he stopped going entirely.

His sleep had been poor for years, but in the past eighteen months it had worsened considerably. He woke most nights in the early hours, alert and convinced, briefly, that he was somewhere he was not. His appetite had diminished. His younger daughter, who visits on weekends, had begun to look at him with an expression he recognised as worry, and it was partly for her sake, he said, that he had finally told his doctor the truth.

What Rajinder hopes for, stated quietly and without much apparent expectation, is to sleep through the night. What he fears is being asked to go back to what he saw.
